A field guide for selling to HVAC owners

The Promise Chain

Win HVAC owners by fixing the spots where their money leaks. Not by saying the word "AI."
STARWELL SI
How to read this book

One idea. Four moves.

This book teaches one thing: how to walk into an HVAC shop, see the real problem, and leave with a paying customer. You do it by finding where money leaks out of the business, then plugging the hole.

It reads in about 40 minutes. Every chapter ends with one thing to do. The pictures repeat on purpose. That's how your brain keeps them.

Part 1 · The Reframe — Chapter 1

He's not selling air conditioners. He's keeping promises.

Forget "HVAC." Your buyer runs a promise machine, and it breaks all day.

The 12-tech owner

A guy runs a shop with twelve techs. Every weekend, every holiday, the emergency calls land on his phone. Not because he wants them. Because he never built a rotation. Ten years later he's fried. He didn't need more customers. He needed a way to say "someone else has this."

If you remember one sentence, make it this: an HVAC owner doesn't sell repairs. He sells promises.

A customer wants a time. A tech needs the right part. The office needs to know what's happening. A supplier has a delivery date. The owner needs to get paid. None of that is the hard part. The hard part is the handoffs, the places where one person hands the job to the next and the ball gets dropped.

One service call crosses nine handoffs before it's done. That's where the money leaks. Not in the wrench work.

13
systems running in every shop
9
handoffs in one service call
3
sizes of owner, each leaks different

Same guy, three jobs

SizeWhat he actually doesWhere it leaks
1–3 techsSells, dispatches, orders parts, invoices, collects. Everything.One missed call wrecks the whole day.
5–15 techsHas an office, but every exception still finds him.He's the backstop for everything.
20+ techsRuns through managers and reports.Problems hide until they cost money.

Here's the thing. The owner's pain isn't "I need AI." It's "I can't leave without it falling apart." Every problem in this book is a promise that got dropped somewhere.

In a nutshell

An owner manages promises, not repairs. The money is in the gaps between people. That's your opening.

Do this

Rewrite the label in your head. Stop thinking "HVAC client." Start thinking "promise-keeper under pressure."

Test yourself

Why does the stress live in the handoffs, not the repair work?

Because the repair is a known skill. The handoffs are where info, ownership, or money silently stall. That's where promises break.

Part 1 · The Reframe — Chapter 2

Stop selling AI. Find the leak.

"We want a chatbot" is almost never the real ask.

The chatbot trap

An owner tells you flat out: "We need a chatbot." Sounds like a done deal. You ask one question: what should it do? Turns out calls go to voicemail at noon, and nobody knows which missed calls ever got called back. The chatbot was never the problem. The missed calls were.

Your job isn't to find a place to stuff AI. It's to find where the business is failing to get a result it cares about, then fix it with the smallest thing that works. AI might be part of the fix. It should never be the reason you picked the problem.

Walk in thinking this, word for word:

"I'm not here to find a spot for AI. I'm here to understand what's stopping this business."

Four questions, in order

Read left to right. "That sounds useful" is not a real problem. Most AI ideas die at gate one or two.

Someone saying "that sounds useful" proves nothing. What proves a problem is a failure that keeps happening, a workaround that costs money, a budget, and a reason to change. We'll hunt for those in Chapter 5.

Don't

Open with "our AI platform" or "we automate your back office." Owners already bought tools that over-promised. You'll sound like the last guy who wasted their money.

In a nutshell

Don't sell AI. Sell the removal of one specific, expensive leak. Reach for AI only when it's the cheapest reliable way.

Do this

Take your pitch ("AI for HVAC!") and rewrite it as a result: "We stop qualified calls from going unanswered." If you can't write it as a result, you don't have a product yet.

Test yourself

Why is "value" and "reliability" two separate things?

A tool can be accurate but not improve the business. And it can look valuable while making bad mistakes. Measure them separately.

Part 2 · Spot the Pattern — Chapter 3

The Promise Chain.

Seven links. Seven places money leaks. This is the whole book in one picture.

A very normal disaster

Customer calls. AC's not cooling. The office books a tech but never grabs the model number or the real symptom. Tech shows up, finds a bad part that isn't on the truck. Office orders it. Part arrives. Nobody books the return visit. Tech finally finishes, but the notes are missing, so the office can't bill. Owner ends up fighting the customer over the charge. The fix was easy. Everything around it broke.

That mess isn't about air conditioning. It's about seven handoffs, and each one is a place money can leak.

The Promise Chain. A job has to survive all seven. Every arrow is a leak point. This is your map.

Read it as a checklist, not a pretty picture:

  • CALL → did anyone answer and write down the right details?
  • DISPATCH → did the right tech with the right part get there on time?
  • FIELD → did the work actually get done right?
  • CLOSEOUT → is the job written up so it can be billed?
  • INVOICE → did the bill go out fast and correct?
  • PAY → did the cash actually land?
  • RETURN → did the customer come back, or leave quietly?
41
problems mapped across this chain
15
of them actually matter
7
links, and the leak is never the same twice
"The best fixes don't touch the equipment. They fix the space between jobs and between people."

Same leak shows up in every shop, just at different strength. A two-tech shop bleeds on missed calls. A fifteen-tech shop bleeds on closeout. A thirty-tech shop bleeds on invoices. The chain is how you find which link is gushing.

In a nutshell

Seven links. Your job is to find the one leaking the most and fix that first.

Do this

Close the book. Draw the seven links from memory. Next to each, write one sign it's leaking. Then do it again in an hour.

Test yourself

Name the seven links.

Call, Dispatch, Field, Closeout, Invoice, Pay, Return.

Part 2 · Spot the Pattern — Chapter 4

Eight things to look for.

You don't need to guess where AI fits. The shop tells you. You just have to see the pattern.

Here's the skill that separates the pros from the guys who cold-call with a slide deck: pattern recognition. When you walk into a shop, you look for the same eight signals. Each one tells you exactly what's broken, what to ask, and whether AI is even the answer.

Most people think patterns are for puzzle nerds. They're wrong. Every giant business ever built started the same way: somebody saw an old need stuck behind friction, and a new cheap tool that removed the friction. Uber did it to rides. Airbnb did it to rooms. You do it to HVAC.

Read left to right, then loop. The need is old. The tool is new. The exchange is what changes.

This is the whole book in eight cards. Memorize them.

1The Sunday phone
SeeThe owner answers his own phone on Sunday night.
MeansEverything still routes to him. No approval limits.
Ask“Which decisions still need your approval after hours?”
AI fitsRules, not AI. Set approval limits and a human owns the exceptions.
2“Only Sarah knows”
SeeSomeone says “only Sarah knows how to do that.”
MeansThe knowledge lives in one person. If she leaves, it's gone.
Ask“What does Sarah know that nobody else does?”
AI fitsWrite Sarah's steps into a required-fields form. That's rules, not AI.
3The 5 phone calls
SeeThe office calls techs five times a day just for status.
MeansThe system doesn't show real progress, so they chase it.
Ask“Which three questions does the office ask techs all day?”
AI fitsShort mobile checkpoints + auto customer updates. Light AI to draft, human to send.
4The part that arrived
SeeA part showed up four days ago. The customer still has no return visit.
MeansNobody owns “parts-pending.” It's a hole with no name on it.
Ask“How does the office know a part arrived, and who books the return?”
AI fitsJob-linked order milestones. Pure automation, no AI.
5The ten dead quotes
SeeTen estimates sent out. Zero followed up.
MeansNobody owns quote follow-up. Money dies in the inbox.
Ask“What happened to the last ten quotes that didn't get approved?”
AI fitsTimed follow-up + AI drafts the nudge, a human sends it.
6The week-late invoice
SeeInvoices go out a week after the job's done.
MeansCloseout is missing data, so billing waits on notes.
Ask“What's the most common thing that stops an invoice?”
AI fitsRequired-field closeout checklist + AI to turn tech notes into a draft. Human reviews.
7The triple ETA call
SeeCustomers call three times to ask “when are you coming?”
MeansNobody tells them until they ask.
Ask“How do you tell a customer you're running late?”
AI fitsEvent-triggered texts with a human override. Rules, mostly.
8The comeback
SeeSame problem comes back. Nobody knows why.
MeansCallbacks aren't classified, so the same mistake repeats.
Ask“What share of callbacks are workmanship, wrong part, or expectation?”
AI fitsA callback label system + AI to spot patterns in notes. Human reviews.
The big idea

Every one of these is a pattern, not a guess. You see the signal, you know the cause, you ask the question, and you know if AI fits before you say a word about it.

Do this

Pick three cards. Write each signal on a sticky note. Tomorrow, in any conversation, listen for them. The first time you hear one in the wild, you'll never forget it.

Test yourself

What's the pattern behind “only Sarah knows”?

Knowledge trapped in one person. The fix is to write it down as a required form, not to build AI.

Part 2 · Spot the Pattern — Chapter 5

Ask like you already know.

The right question does two jobs. It finds the leak, and it makes you look like you've been doing this for years.

Two openers, same shop

Guy A asks: "Do you need AI?" Eyes glaze over. Guy B asks: "How many jobs are sitting there waiting on a part with no return visit booked?" The owner leans forward. Guy B just named a pain nobody else ever saw.

Owners don't buy AI. They buy the feeling of being understood. The right question gives you both: it finds the leak, and it proves you belong in the room.

Listen like this

  • Let them finish. One question at a time.
  • Use the pause. Don't fill every silence.
  • Repeat it back: "Let me make sure I got this right..."
  • Never blame their staff.
  • Don't defend your idea while you're still learning.

Ten questions that open the door

#QuestionWhat it reveals
1Walk me through yesterday. What happened that wasn't on the calendar?The real day, not the brochure.
2What's the first thing you check each morning, and what are you worried you'll see?His biggest fear.
3Show me the oldest open job. What's it waiting on, and who owns it?Where work stalls.
4How many calls went unanswered last week? How do you know?Whether he can even see the leak.
5Which three questions does the office ask techs over and over all day?Status-chasing, the hidden tax.
6Tell me about the last second trip a tech made. What would've stopped it?Callback root cause.
7What's the most common thing that stops an invoice from going out?The closeout leak.
8What happened to the last ten quotes nobody approved?Dead-quote leak.
9If you took seven days off, what breaks first, and who calls you?His real bottleneck.
10If one problem vanished tomorrow, what would you notice first?How he'll measure success. That's your hook.

Hear the signal, then hunt the cause

You hearAsk next
"We enter it in three places.""Which one's the real record, and why the others?"
"We're always waiting.""Waiting on who, for what, how long?"
"I check everything myself.""What are you catching, and how often?"
"We tried software already.""Show me where it broke down."
"We just need a chatbot.""What work should it do, and how's that done now?"
In a nutshell

Ask about specific things that already happened, not opinions about the future. The question that names his unspoken pain wins the room.

Do this

Pick three questions. Write them in your own words. Rehearse one "repeat it back" line out loud.

Test yourself

Why ask about a past event, not "would this help you?"

Past events show real behavior and real cost. "Would this help" just gets a polite yes.

Part 3 · Where AI Actually Fits — Chapter 6

Rules first. AI second. A person always.

Most of what an HVAC owner needs isn't AI. It's a rule that fires every time.

The reminder that should've been a rule

A shop's invoices go out late because nothing says "flag a job with missing notes." They don't need a robot to read tech chatter. They need a required field. Slap AI on a problem a rule already solves, and you look like every other overpriced vendor.

One rule to live by: never let a model make a decision a simple rule can handle. Sort every job into three buckets.

Three buckets

BucketUse it forWhy
RulesConfirmations, reminders, required fields, status alerts, approval limits, recurring maintenance.Always works. Never makes things up. Cheap.
AI + a humanTranscribing calls, reading a model number off a photo, drafting customer updates, searching manuals.AI does the draft, a person approves before anything ships.
No AISafety diagnosis, refrigerant, permits, emergency triage, financing, pricing.The cost of a mistake is too high.

The five places to start

PilotWhat it doesLink it plugs
AMissed-call recovery — unanswered calls land in one queue with an owner and a response time.CALL
BEstimate follow-up — every quote gets an owner and a next date.INVOICE → RETURN
CInvoice-ready closeout — required fields before a job can be billed.CLOSEOUT
DDispatch recovery — live status, a person approves changes.DISPATCH
EParts-pending — orders, arrival, and return visit all tied to one job.FIELD

Notice what all five share: a named owner, a clear next step, and a human in the loop. None of them is "let the AI run the shop." That's exactly what an owner respects.

In a nutshell

Rules first, AI second, a person always. Use the simplest thing that reliably works.

Do this

For each of the five pilots, write which bucket it belongs in. If you can't place one, you don't understand it well enough to sell it yet.

Test yourself

Name the three buckets and one job in each.

Rules (invoice reminders). AI + human (reading a serial off a photo). No AI (safety diagnosis, financing).

Part 3 · Where AI Actually Fits — Chapter 7

The test that can't lose.

Don't pitch a platform. Pitch one workflow, a number attached, a person in the loop, and an off-ramp.

The whole business vs one workflow

One vendor pitches "an AI chief of staff for your whole company." Vague, expensive, scary. Another says: "Let's route your missed calls into one queue and call every one back in 15 minutes, for two weeks. If it doesn't book more jobs, we stop." Same tech. One sounds like a bet, the other like an experiment you'd be dumb to refuse.

Owners have been burned by big software. The way past that wall is to make the ask small, bounded, and reversible.

Pick the thing that gates everything

Don't fix the loudest complaint. Fix the thing that's limiting the whole business. If techs are already fully booked, faster quotes just pile up more demand you can't serve.

The whole business moves at the speed of its narrowest step. Find it, improve it, then find the next one.

Write the problem down first

The template

For [a specific person], when [a specific situation], [the problem] stops [a result they want]. Today they handle it with [the workaround], which costs [a real number]. We'll test whether [the fix] moves [a metric], within [limits].

If you can't fill every blank, you don't have a pilot. You have a hope.

Agree on this before you start

Before day one
  • The one workflow and the people in it.
  • The baseline — how it performs today, measured.
  • The one number that has to move.
  • Guardrails and who approves what.
  • Stop conditions and scale conditions.
Don't

Test only the easy happy-path cases. A pilot that never touches a messy exception proves nothing. Owners respect you more for finding a failure early than for hiding one.

In a nutshell

The win isn't "a smaller chatbot." It's one complete workflow, with a measured number and a person in charge — small enough to say yes to, real enough to prove itself.

Do this

Write one full problem statement for the leak you'd most want to fix. Fill every blank. The blank that stumps you is your next question.

Test yourself

Why agree on stop conditions and scale conditions up front?

So you decide on evidence, not excitement after a good demo. Pre-agreed limits stop you from chasing a loser.

Part 4 · Win — Chapter 8

Numbers that survive Monday.

The difference between a vendor and a partner is whether your numbers hold up when the owner squints at them.

The ROI that melted

A vendor claims "we'll save you 20 hours a week." Monday comes. The owner asks: "saved for what, and where's the cash?" The number dissolves. Because time saved isn't money. A tech who finishes early might just idle longer, not bill more.

Sell the number that survives. The honest math is:

Net value

value = saved money + new money − full cost

And "full cost" includes the human review time, training, and fixing the mistakes.

Four things not to confuse

Don't confuseThe truth
Sales with profitCount what's left after delivery costs, not the sticker price.
Time saved with cash savedSay whether it cuts overtime, avoids a hire, or just adds slack.
A good draft with a good resultA perfect draft only matters if the work gets done faster.
A pilot lift with causeHVAC is weather-driven. Don't credit yourself for a heat wave.

Measure against a before, or it's a story

You can't prove a change without a "before." Grab the baseline first. These are the numbers owners actually trust:

  • Missed-call rate — calls not answered live.
  • Lead-to-booked rate — inquiries that turn into booked jobs.
  • First-time fix rate — jobs done without a second trip.
  • Callback rate — return trips, split by cause.
  • Completion-to-invoice lag — days from done to billed.
  • Job gross margin — money left after direct labor and parts.
In a nutshell

Measure against a baseline, count full cost, and never claim cash from time you didn't prove.

Do this

Write the value equation on a sticky note. Under "full cost," list one thing you'd forget: technician review time.

Test yourself

Give one example of a good draft that's not a good result.

A perfect invoice summary the office still has to check against the tech's notes. The draft is great, the invoice didn't go out any faster.

Part 4 · Win — Chapter 9

Sell the result, not the robot.

Nobody wakes up wanting "an AI platform." They wake up wanting the leak gone.

Two sentences, one product

"We offer an AI-powered operational intelligence platform." Silence. "We turn your messy call-ins into ready-to-approve quotes, with pricing kept in human hands." Now he's nodding. Same thing. One version names a person, a job, and a boundary. The other names a technology.

Positioning is just explaining your value against what the owner already does — which is usually a spreadsheet, a part-timer, or "just keep suffering."

QuestionAnswer it
AlternativeWhat are we replacing or improving?
DifferenceWhy is this better than the current way?
Who caresWhich person (dispatcher, CSR, owner) benefits most?
ProofWhat evidence backs the claim?
Worth itWhy is the change worth the disruption?

What they'll pay for, and what they won't

They pay to removeThey won't buy
A real leak in qualified calls. Quote follow-up gaps. Invoice lag. Unpaid callbacks. A parts job that stalls. An after-hours burden.A dashboard nobody checks. A second system with double entry. Generic AI chat. Anything that slows a tech down. An unproven ROI claim.
"Sell progress, not AI. Help them get somewhere. Don't try to make them want your features."
In a nutshell

Name a person, a job, and a boundary — never a technology. "Review-ready quotes, human-approved" beats "AI platform" every time.

Do this

Write your one-liner two ways, side by side: the "AI platform" version and the "result" version. Read both out loud. Delete the first one.

Test yourself

Why is one internal win not proof of a sellable product?

It proves value for one company, not that others share the problem, are reachable, or can justify the price.

Close · Chapter 10

The 30-day plan.

From "never met an HVAC owner" to "a signed pilot and a next step."

Thirty days. Five moves. One bounded test. This turns everything in this book into real, provable work.

DaysDo this
1–5Interview owners. Pick three sizes (small, medium, large). Use the ten questions on real recent jobs. Get permission before touching any records.
6–10Shadow the office. Watch dispatch. Log every status call, missing closeout, aged quote, parts stall, and owner escalation. Write the root cause, not just the complaint.
11–15Talk to the field. Interview techs and managers. Compare their story against timestamps and notes.
16–20Set the baseline. Nail the numbers. Split "software setup" from "missing policy" from "bad data" from "real gap."
21–25Pilot one workflow. One bounded test. Human in the loop. Pre-agreed success and stop rules.
26–30Review the evidence. Sit with owner, dispatcher, and techs. Decide: keep, change, or stop. On data, not vibes.
The rule

Before you build or recommend anything, know the exact workflow, how often it fails, the real cost, the current workaround, who owns it, and what would make the owner pay to change it. You're not selling tech. You're removing a real brake on the business.

Close · Chapter 11

The one-page checklist.

Answer all fifteen before you build or pitch anything. If you can't, you're not ready.

The whole book on one page. Run it top to bottom every time, and you'll never build something nobody needs.

The fifteen questions
  1. What result are we trying to get?
  2. Who feels the problem, and who owns the result?
  3. What real cases prove it exists?
  4. What does it cost, and which parts are guesses?
  5. Is it a blocker, or just annoying?
  6. How is it handled today?
  7. Why did the last fix fail?
  8. What simpler option did we skip?
  9. Why does this job need AI at all?
  10. What data and permission do we need?
  11. What must stay under a human?
  12. What assumption could kill this?
  13. What's the smallest test?
  14. What numbers and stop rules are agreed up front?
  15. Who owns running it and fixing it when it breaks?
"Move from result, to observed problem, to a tested fix. Keep the solution smaller than your ambition until the evidence says grow."
The last line

An HVAC owner wants fewer dropped promises, fewer pointless return trips, faster cash, and the ability to leave without it falling apart. Win by proving you remove one repeated, costly handoff, with less pain than the workaround it replaces.
